summary: Sirach 19 begins with warnings about self-destructive habits: drunkenness, reckless sexual conduct, shallow trust, delight in wickedness, and gossip. It then gives practical instruction for handling rumors by keeping silence, questioning a friend or neighbor before believing accusations, and correcting before threatening. The chapter closes by distinguishing true wisdom from clever wickedness and by warning that deceit can hide behind outward humility until opportunity appears.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Sirach’s concern that wisdom is tested in ordinary speech, trust, correction, and judgment. It also links wisdom with fear of the Lord and doing the law, not merely with intelligence or social cleverness.

context.author: Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew book into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jewish readers who wanted to live according to the law.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal study, and daily life taking place within a Greek-speaking Mediterranean world.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction made of compact maxims, paired lines, vivid comparisons, and practical moral teaching.

outline.heading: Habits that waste a life
outline.note: The chapter warns against drunkenness, despising small things, reckless sexual conduct, hasty trust, sin, delight in wickedness, and gossip.

outline.heading: Do not pass on what you hear
outline.note: The teacher urges silence about reports and pictures gossip as a painful word trapped inside a fool.

outline.heading: Question before you accuse
outline.note: A friend or neighbor may not have done or said what is reported, and even a real wrong may be corrected before threats begin.

outline.heading: Wisdom, fear, and law
outline.note: The World English Bible leaves verses 18, 19, and 21 blank. The remaining sayings bind wisdom to fear of the Lord and doing the law, rather than to knowledge of wickedness.

outline.heading: Clever deceit and visible character
outline.note: The final sayings warn against unjust subtlety, false mourning, hidden deceit, and the way a person’s outward conduct may reveal character.

keyVerses.text: Never repeat what is told you, and you won’t lose anything.
keyVerses.why: This sentence states the chapter’s central counsel about refusing to spread reports.

keyVerses.text: Question a friend; for many times there is slander. Don’t trust every word.
keyVerses.why: It gives the chapter’s method for handling accusation: ask before believing or repeating it.

keyVerses.text: All wisdom is the fear of the Lord. In all wisdom is the doing of the law.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the chapter’s definition of wisdom in reverence and practiced obedience rather than mere cleverness.

keyVerses.text: Better is one who has little understanding, and fears God, than one who has much intelligence and transgresses the law.
keyVerses.why: It sharpens the contrast between limited understanding joined to reverence and great intelligence joined to disobedience.

themes: Wisdom and fear of the Lord

questions.question: What problem does the chapter address first?
questions.answer: It begins with habits that gradually destroy a person’s life: drunkenness, despising small things, reckless sexual behavior, shallow trust, sin, and delight in wickedness. The sayings are brief, but they present self-control as part of wisdom rather than as a separate topic.

questions.question: What does “despises small things” mean here?
questions.answer: The chapter does not define the phrase, so it should be read cautiously. In context, it sits beside drunkenness and gradual downfall, suggesting a warning that small neglected choices can become a path of loss “little by little.”

questions.question: Why does the chapter spend so much space on gossip?
questions.answer: Verses 6-12 treat gossip as something that increases wickedness and damages trust. The teacher’s advice is blunt: do not repeat what you hear, whether it concerns a friend or an enemy, unless silence itself would make you guilty.

questions.question: Does “Unless it is a sin to you, don’t reveal it” mean every secret must be kept?
questions.answer: The line gives a general rule against exposing what one hears, but it also names an exception: a situation where silence would be a sin. The chapter does not list examples, so readers should not use the verse as a blanket command to hide harm or wrongdoing.

questions.question: What should someone do before believing a bad report?
questions.answer: The chapter says to question the person involved. It repeats the point with both friend and neighbor, then adds that there is often slander and that one should not trust every word.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say someone may slip “not from the heart”?
questions.answer: The saying recognizes that a person can fail in speech without that failure expressing settled intent. It does not excuse every wrong word, since the next verse still calls for reproof, but it slows the rush from hearing a report to assuming motive.

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by “the fear of the Lord”?
questions.answer: In this chapter, fear of the Lord is tied directly to wisdom and doing the law. The phrase points to reverent allegiance expressed in conduct, not simply an emotion of fright.

questions.question: Why is intelligence not enough in this chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter distinguishes wisdom from knowledge of wickedness and from the prudence of sinners. It even says a person with little understanding who fears God is better than someone with much intelligence who transgresses the law.

questions.question: How should readers handle verses 18, 19, and 21 when they are blank here?
questions.answer: The World English Bible leaves verses 18, 19, and 21 blank. Sirach survives in different textual forms, and editions can differ in wording and verse numbering. Other editions may include additional lines or number the passage differently.

glossary.def: Talk about another person that the chapter warns against repeating or carrying inside oneself like a painful burden.
A damaging report that may be false or unfair; the chapter says there is often slander and tells readers not to trust every word.
The person one may need to question and reprove before moving to threats or judgment.
The instruction the chapter connects with true wisdom, fear of the Lord, and faithful conduct.
